titolo: Jensen Huang: Trump Wants Him Back. Nvidia's Stock Crashes 12%
angolo: Trump asks for a 'second chance' for Huang on the very day the market loses about $485 billion on a reported SEC accounting probe. Who decides whether Huang returns: the President, the board or the markets?
descrizione: Jensen Huang: Trump Wants Him Back. Nvidia's Stock Crashes 12%. On Friday, President Trump publicly asked Nvidia to give its ousted co-founder a second chance, while the board says it will not reinstate him. The same day, Nvidia shares fell about 12 to 14 percent after Reuters reported, citing two people briefed on the matter, that SEC staff are examining potential accounting issues. We walk through what is confirmed, what is only reported, and what comes next: Congress, California, and the search for a new CEO.

scene.testo: Friday. The President of the United States asks a company to take back its founder.
Hours later, Nvidia loses roughly half a trillion dollars in market value in a single day, according to market reports.
And the man at the center of it all? He is due to testify before Congress.
Can a President bring back the man who resigned as Nvidia's CEO?
First, the words. Here is what Trump told reporters on Friday.
He also called Huang a good man who made some bad decisions, according to AFP.
He said Nvidia should accept an apology and let Huang go back to work.
His case: Huang built something with Blackwell, Nvidia's most advanced chips.
But there is a problem. The board has already answered.
Chairman Harvey Jones said it on the earnings call this week.
Note: that line was spoken by chairman Harvey Jones, as CNBC reports. Remember it.
Huang offered to return, in a post on X on Tuesday, according to Al Jazeera.
He said he would be honored to return, according to The Hill and the Wall Street Journal.
In a moment: the number that rattled Wall Street on Friday.
But first, how did a founder end up outside his own company?
THE FOUNDER
Huang was born in Taipei, Taiwan, in 1963.
Mapping where it began: Taiwan, the heart of the chip supply chain.
In 1993 he co-founded Nvidia in Sunnyvale, California, with two partners.
Over three decades, it became one of the world's most valuable companies.
Its chips power the artificial intelligence boom.
In October, Trump handed Huang the National Medal of Science.
A month later, he was out.

visivo.testo: A MONTH LATER, HE WAS OUT.

scene.testo: THE FALL
November twelfth: Nvidia announces Huang has resigned as CEO and left the board.
CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. Harvey Jones became first-ever chair.
It followed reports of relationships with two women, one allegedly a Chinese spy.
Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife, The Hill reports.
The woman in question worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer.
Where Megaspeed sits: Singapore, one of Asia's main data center hubs.
Megaspeed is being investigated for potentially diverting restricted chips to China, CNBC reports.
Huang's representatives and Nvidia have not been reported to confirm any wrongdoing. It remains under investigation.
Since its October record, the stock has fallen by almost half, according to market reports.
Now to the number I promised. It came Friday afternoon.
Reuters reported, citing two people briefed, that SEC enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia.
Reuters could not say when the inquiry began, or which issues it covers.
The SEC declined to comment. Nvidia did not immediately respond.
The stock fell about twelve to fourteen percent, its worst day since the DeepSeek drop of January 2025.
Other outlets put the drop between twelve and fourteen percent, depending on the time.
Bloomberg reports it was the seventh straight loss. Separately, other outlets say the stock lost about 23 percent this week, its worst week since October 2008.
An SEC inquiry is not a finding of wrongdoing. Many end without action.

visivo.testo: AN INQUIRY IS NOT A FINDING.

scene.testo: So what is the SEC reportedly looking at? Here is the thread analysts are pulling.
Last year, Nvidia changed how it reports revenue by region.
It switched from billing addresses to customers' headquarters. Singapore vanished from the breakdown.
As recently as mid-2025, Singapore was 22 percent of revenue: about ten point two billion dollars in the quarter ended July 2025.
The Financial Times reported that about one hundred and four billion dollars was booked through Nvidia's Singapore subsidiary in 2025.
Nvidia said at the time the change reflected its geographic mix more accurately.
Whether any of this is in the SEC's scope is unconfirmed. Neither the SEC nor Nvidia has said.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that the SEC probe includes whether disclosures misled investors.
THE WITNESS STAND
Also Friday: a spokesperson for Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott says Huang will testify publicly before the panel.
A spokesperson for Chairman Tim Scott confirmed it. No date has been announced.
Scott initially asked for December third, and told CNBC he hopes to hear from Huang before Christmas.
Scott has also said he has concerns about Nvidia's controls. Here is what he told CNBC.
That quote is from Senator Tim Scott, as quoted by UPI.
He is due before three House panels too, in a closed-door interview on December first.
Lawmakers will question him about alleged Chinese espionage and chip export rules, UPI reports.
CBS reports he agreed under the threat of a subpoena.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also been asked to appear.
Next: a ghost from two decades ago that resurfaced Friday.
A COMPLAINT FROM 2007
Bloomberg reports two Nvidia employees complained about Huang's behavior about two decades ago.
The allegations appear in a California lawsuit filed in 2007.
Nvidia's first in-house lawyer said he saw Huang verbally abuse and intimidate staff.
The company cited performance issues for firing him, according to court documents.
Huang's representatives say the allegations are from long ago and do not represent him.
Huang has previously said he would rather push people toward greatness. Fortune reported his words in 2024.
Meanwhile, some employees have urged the board to bring him back, CNBC reports.
One senior employee reportedly warned of losing irreplaceable talent.
THE SEARCH
Meanwhile, the board is looking for a new chief executive.
The Financial Times reported the board approached Arm CEO Rene Haas.
Bloomberg says recruiters at Heidrick and Struggles approached him, citing a person familiar. Arm declined to comment.
Haas spent seven years at Nvidia, from 2006 to 2013, before joining Arm in 2013.
Of Huang, he said at a tech conference in Austin on Wednesday: he is a legend.
The board says speculation about individual candidates is premature, as Reuters reported last Friday.
THE OTHER CLOCKS
California's attorney general served Nvidia an investigative subpoena on Thursday.
That is Attorney General Rob Bonta, quoted in his office's statement.
The map of pressure now runs from Oakland to Washington to Singapore.
WHAT NOW
A President's wish is not a directive, one outlet noted. The board is not obliged to follow.
Also on Friday, Treasury Secretary Bessent said Trump had not discussed Huang with Xi.
Trump then said he did discuss Huang with Xi, and quoted Xi as calling Huang a brilliant man.
Interim CEO Kress told staff: let's move forward, a person present told CNBC.
The company also reported strong results this week, with revenue of about one hundred sixteen billion dollars.
Strong results. Yet the stock still fell, seven sessions in a row.
So three forces now decide Huang's future: a president, a board, and the market.

visivo.testo: A PRESIDENT. A BOARD. A MARKET.

scene.testo: Which one wins, we do not know yet. The story is still moving. Subscribe, and stay with us.
